1.1: 1.1 Argument. The Philippians are Macedonians. These, having received the word of truth, persevered in the faith, and did not receive false apostles. This he praises, writing to them from Rome from prison through Epaphroditus. Paul. After his custom he puts the greeting first; then gives thanks to God for them, imploring greater goods for them, that growing in virtues they may come to perfection. Then he admonishes patience in tribulations by the example of himself and Christ, afterward that they beware of the wiles of the false apostles; finally he interposes a moral admonition, and near the end says he rejoices over the gift they had sent him at Rome through Epaphroditus. Timothy. He adds him, because he was about to send him to them: for this reason commending him in a way, that they receive from him the same things he writes. Servants. He said servants, that they too may bear hard things for the Lord. Of Christ. That they may stand against the false apostles.
1.3: 1.3 I give thanks to my God. As if he said: Do what you do, because such things they are, for which I praise God.
1.5: 1.5 In the communication. By which you made your goods common, in exalting the Gospel.
1.6: 1.6 Being confident. As: I pray that you stand, and I am confident that this very thing is done by you that I pray for, and not another; but see that I am not confident in vain. Will perfect. He who begins that we may will, cooperates with the willing in perfecting.
1.7: 1.7 As it is right for me. So I give thanks, pray and trust, as it is just to think, that is, so to will. And he explains the cause, because I have you in my heart, I desire good for you, whether I am bound, knowing that you too are bound, or defending the Gospel, which you also do.
1.8: 1.8 I long for you all, etc. That is, with the inmost love of Christ, that you may be perfectly loved by him, or that you may love God and neighbors with the affection with which Christ, who laid down his life. Or this refers to what he said above, that he desires them to be partakers of his joy. And he determines how, namely by the love of Christ, not human, that he may have partakers in God.
1.10: 1.10 That you may approve the better things. That is, that your charity may abound in knowledge, that you may know how to prove and discern not only what is evil and good, but also among good things which are better, that after the proving you may be sincere in yourselves, without works of corruption, and as to your neighbor, without offense.
1.11: 1.11 Filled with the fruit, etc. That is, with the reward of justice, so that you may be the glory and praise of God, that it be said for you: God is wonderful in his saints, Psalm 67.
1.12: 1.12 Now I would have you know, etc. Hitherto he has spoken in common; from here he sets down specially what urges tolerance, namely, I give thanks for you: I am confident. But I would have you know, etc., as if he said: Since you are so perfect, persevere and beware, lest the tribulations at hand diminish this your perfection, but look to my example.
1.13: 1.13 So that my bonds, etc. Because I bear any evils patiently, it is plain that it is not the crime of falsehood that a just vengeance strikes in me, but a certain virtue of truth which the strength of endurance magnifies.
1.14: 1.14 More bold, etc. For his constancy so encouraged many that they did not fear to preach the Gospel.
1.17: 1.17 Some, etc. Convicted by me in debate, they preach as they think they ought to preach, being convicted. Out of contention. From private hatred, which they once brought against me, and were confuted. And lest they seem corrected, he adds: Not sincerely.
1.18: 1.18 What then? He does not forbid hirelings, but permits them, because even they are useful for some things. But I also will rejoice. Therefore I rejoice over my evils, or over the progress of the Gospel, because from that comes salvation for me.
1.21: 1.21 For to me to live is Christ, etc. As if he said: Rightly I magnify Christ whether by life or by death, because to me to live is Christ, that is, life to me here by faith and hope, and in the future by sight. For this life he gave his mortal body, that he might receive it immortal forever, whence he adds and to die is gain.
1.22: 1.22 And if to live, etc. Christ is to me to live, that I may magnify him. If this is so, then I know not which to choose, to die or to live. As: Unless there were this fruit, there is no doubt I would choose to die that I might have Christ as my reward: and so, doubt not to die for Christ.
1.24: 1.24 But to abide, etc. Behold, he chooses not what is better for himself, but what is expedient for many, for the sake of charity, which is to be chosen before all things.
1.25: 1.25 And joy of faith, etc. That is: That we may rejoice in your faith, or that you may rejoice in faith, advancing in it. Which is not except where there is a clean conscience.
1.28: 1.28 And this from God, etc. Even what you suffer is not from yourselves, but from God: because for the merit of Christ who obeyed the Father, this among other graces has been given to you.
1.29: 1.29 Not only, etc. Both therefore pertain to the grace of God, both the faith of believers and the endurance of sufferers, because he said both are given.
1.30: 1.30 Having the same conflict which you have seen in me. When I was stripped and beaten on account of the woman with the spirit of Python from whom I cast out the evil spirit, who brought great gain to her masters.
2.1: 2.1 If there be any consolation, etc. If you wish to have consolation in the things of Christ, that is in the remission of sins and in other gifts; or: if you wish to console me, if there is any solace of charity to you, that is if you wish the charity of the churches, which pray and do good for the brethren, to be a solace and comfort to you in your adversities. If any fellowship of the spirit. On account of this fellowship those upon whom the Holy Spirit first came spoke with the tongues of all nations. If any bowels. That is if you have an affection of piety toward me. I do not say the very compassion, that is the exhibition of mercy. If these, I say, you wish to profit you, fulfill my joy, that is be humble, of one mind, which you will be if you are of the same mind, etc.
2.3: 2.3 Nothing through contention. Note that there were contentions among them. Superior, etc. Truly this is to be thought, because there can be in another something hidden by which he is superior, even if our own good by which we seem superior is not hidden.
2.4: 2.4 Not the things that are his own. Here he teaches how they may avoid contention and vainglory, and how they may deem others superior, namely if they consider not their own goods but those of others.
2.5: 2.5 For let this mind be, etc. As if he said: Let each seek not his own advantage but that of others, as Christ did. I invite you to patience and humility. For you ought to be minded in yourselves as was in Christ. As Christ sought not his own things but ours, so let us bear one another's burdens.
2.6: 2.6 Who being in the form. He sets lofty things about Christ first, that those in whom there is place for abasement may not disdain to be humbled. Not robbery. By usurping what was not his, like the devil and the first man. Or, he did not think himself equal to God according to the humanity, which would be to commit robbery, that is, to presume what is not his own. But emptied himself. The height having been shown, he adds of the humility. Augustine, Enchiridion, ch. 35 and 36. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc., down to it was brought about that the man Christ could have no sin. The form of a servant. Not losing the form of God: the form of a servant was added, the form of God did not depart: He emptied himself. To empty himself is to show himself visible from the greatness of his invisibility.
2.7: 2.7 Made. According to the form of a servant, he who was uncreated according to the form of God, and also in his own Habit. That is, in conversation.
2.8: 2.8 He humbled, etc. CHRYSOSTOM. Of his own will the Son obeyed the Father, not as to servile, etc., down to that he honored the Father most of all.
2.9: 2.9 Wherefore. The humility of Christ having been shown, which appeared most in the passion, now he shows his brightness, and what and how much humility deserves.
2.10: 2.10 That at the name. Here he reveals to whom the name of God has been given, to whom every creature bends the knee, that is to God. But perhaps it might be said that the man was God by adoption, and so Christ would be partly true God, who would partly be adopted. But to an adopted God the creature does not bend the knee, but to the true. It is clear, however, that Christ is true God, to whom the knee is bent, not adopted.
2.11: 2.11 That the Lord, etc. Which some here deny, saying: How can it be that a man be in the glory of God the Father? but if he is adopted, a man-God cannot be in the glory of God the Father.
2.13: 2.13 For it is God. Nor even concerning the perseverance in good did God will his saints to glory in their own strength, but in himself: who gives them not only such help as he gave the first man, without which they cannot persevere if they will, but also works in them to will, so that since they will not persevere unless they both can and will, both the possibility and the will of persevering are given them by the largesse of divine grace. For so much is their will kindled by the Holy Spirit that they can because they so will: they so will because God works that they will.
2.14: 2.14 And do all things. He joins patience to humility.
2.15: 2.15 Of a perverse nation, etc. That is of the wicked, who deprave and pervert the right order. Who are called a nation, because they are not born again of water and the Holy Spirit. As lights. Well does he compare the saints to lights. For as night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly iniquity does not darken the minds of the faithful clinging to the heaven of holy Scripture.
2.20: 2.20 For I have no man, etc. At this time many are hirelings with the Apostle, but sons or shepherds none but Timothy.
2.21: 2.21 All, etc. These are the hirelings, who are to be tolerated, because they have in their mouth the same things as the shepherds, who surely are to be loved. But thieves who preach false things, and robbers who kill, are to be shunned.
3.1: 3.1 Finally. As: Hitherto I have instructed you how you ought to stand in the battle against tribulations, for the rest I warn you of the false apostles, that you receive not legal observances from them, but believe the faith of Christ alone sufficient. He begins on the sincerity of faith. To write. That the writing may last longer than the utterance.
3.3: 3.3 For we, etc. That is: We have the circumcision: this the Apostle meant to say: We are justice. For circumcision is justice. He commends it more by saying we are the circumcision, that is justice, than by saying we are circumcised, that is just: yet so that when he says it is justice we understand the just. Who serve the Spirit of God, or, God, etc. He notes the Spirit of the Lord to whom latria is rendered, but that service is to be rendered to the Creator alone. There is another service, by which we are commanded to serve one another through charity, which in Greek is called dulia. And have no confidence in the flesh. He serves in the flesh who hopes to please God by carnal things. But when the flesh itself is made subject to the spirit by good works, we serve God in spirit, who tame the flesh that the spirit may obey God.
3.4: 3.4 Though I also, etc. Lest the Apostle seem to despise in others what he has not, and to be unable to trust in the flesh, he adds: Though, etc.
3.5: 3.5 Of the tribe of Benjamin. The tribe of Benjamin clung to Judah, not departing from the temple, when the division was made under the servant of Solomon. For then the tribe of Judah, which was royal, and the tribe of Benjamin, and the tribe of Levi, which was priestly, remained together, not departing from Jerusalem and the temple.
3.7: 3.7 For Christ. Lest I should show the coming of Christ either not yet done or superfluous. For all these things were vain hindrances to approaching grace.
3.8: 3.8 Yea doubtless I count. Not only for the sake of having Christ did I so judge, but even if I could not attain him. For this only, namely the knowledge we have of Jesus, surpassing other knowledges. As dung. As: Not only losses of goods, but things that defile him who now observes them: and this in order that in the future they may have Christ as their reward: and here I may be a member in him: which cannot otherwise be done unless I esteem those things as dung.
3.9: 3.9 My own justice, etc. If justice is of the law, how is it yours? Did you impose the law on yourself? God gave and imposed the law. God commanded you to obey his law. But it is yours also, because you presume on the law, thinking by your own will you can fulfill the law. CHRYSOSTOM. Rightly he said: Not having my own justice, etc., down to what has proceeded from our own zeal. But that, etc. AUGUSTINE. Which obtains from God, which takes away fear, etc., down to is wholly to be taken away according to the shadow of legal figures. Justice in faith. Justice is a being in faith, and as it was born of faith, so it has no existence except in faith.
3.10: 3.10 That I may know. He adds a commendation of faith, by the many things it does. For it makes us know perfectly in the other life God, who is here believed. And to have the resurrection, which our resurrection is the power and efficacy of the resurrection of Christ. And in this life to have fellowship in suffering: for except through faith no one would suffer so much; and the configuration of death, that is that we die as he did, if need be.
3.11: 3.11 If by any means I may attain. Ascribing to God what he gives me, thereby to come to the resurrection. Or, I may meet Christ in the judgment which belongs to the saints alone, coming first to the true and glorious resurrection, which is not among the dead, but far from the dead: because though all rise in the day of judgment, only the just shall be gloriously changed, and meet the Lord in the air, carried by angels. The impious will remain on earth until they receive the terrible sentence of the judge. Not that I have already attained. He says this of himself, lest those whom he praises be puffed up as men, but add labor, as he does who is so great. But I follow after, etc. Not with steps of the body, but with affections of the mind and the manners of life, that I may be a perfect possessor of justice: who, advancing by the straight road from day to day by spiritual renewal, am now a perfect traveler in the same justice. For he was a perfect traveler, but not yet a perfect arriver at the perfection of the road itself. If by any means I may comprehend. He says this because it is difficult. And lest it seem superfluous to suffer so much, when he has faith and other goods, he adds: Deservedly I labor so much for that glory, because I do not say that I have already received anything: for if I have received any glory, it is nothing in comparison with the future. Or if I have received anything, as of the knowledge of Christ, I do not say that I am perfect in it. And if so of me, what of me compared with others?
3.13: 3.13 Forgetting the things that are behind. Former deeds, not because evil, but small for merit, but stretching to the better, that he may ever advance to better.
3.14: 3.14 I press toward. Even until I come to the appointed good. Of the high calling. That is of eternal life, to which God calls, and so it is a worthy thing, etc.
3.15: 3.15 Let us therefore as many as are perfect. It is to be known that the justice by which the just man lives by faith is true justice, which, though not undeservedly called perfect in some just men according to the capacity of this life, is yet small compared to that great one, which the equality of the angels began: which he who had not yet, both on account of that which was already in him called himself perfect, and on account of that which was still lacking imperfect. But this lesser justice makes merit, that greater makes reward. Therefore he who does not follow this does not attain that. And if you be otherwise minded. That is, if you have thought out anything better for the worship of God, know that this also is the gift of God, because he will reveal it to you. But lest any presumption arise from it, he adds: to which we have attained, that we be of the same mind: that is not to be wise outside the rule of discipline, but what is common and modest in evangelical truth. Nevertheless unto. Now we are imperfect, now we are minded differently, but yet it is necessary that we all be of the same mind about that to which we have attained by faith and knowledge, and abide in the same rule. That is, let us fulfill it in work.
3.18: 3.18 Enemies of the cross. Who bring in carnal observances assert the cross superfluous.
3.19: 3.19 Whose God is their belly. As if salvation were in food, so that the belly is a god, and they glory in the shameful parts of the circumcised, which is to be wise in earthly things, and whatever they do, they do for the belly. Or they make a god of the foods that belong to the belly: while they say these justify men, and their glory is in such things, whence they can be confounded and ashamed, while they say they are justified through temporal things. And so their temporal glory will lead them to eternal confusion.
3.20: 3.20 Our conversation. That is, in living and understanding let us be like the angels. Whence also, that is, besides the advantages we already have, we also look for the Lord.
4.1: 4.1 My joy, and consolation. That is, through whom I am gladdened in the present and shall be crowned in the future. For when the disciples are victors in the contest, the master will be worthy of the crown.
4.2: 4.2 I beseech Euodia, etc. I admonish all, but specially Euodia and Syntyche: because these religious women were wont to receive the preachers.
4.3: 4.3 Names. Those who are distinguished by merits will have different mansions in the eternal house. Whence: In my Father's house there are many mansions, John 14. The book of life. Predestination, in which all who are to be saved are predestined. As: Be not, O Philippians, grieved that I have not named all of you individually in my epistle, because though you are not written in it, you are yet contained in the book of life.
4.4: 4.4 Rejoice, etc. Having rejoiced in their faith and works, the Apostle, that they may be the more eager, wishes those advancing in this zeal to rejoice in the Lord, and repeats it, to show that he truly rejoices in them.
4.5: 4.5 Modesty. That is a right measure, that all joy be in the Lord, and that others learn this through you. Or let your modesty be known to all the faithful and unbelievers, that they may imitate and be unable to reprehend. The Lord is nigh, that is, ready to give whatever is needed in things spiritual or temporal. Be nothing solicitous and fearful. But your petitions for those things you wish to obtain.
4.6: 4.6 But in every prayer. Prayer and supplication are in common for oneself or others, about anything, but petition is made for things specially necessary. Let be made known. This knowledge comes by assiduity and watchfulness of prayer. Then at last peace guards the hearts in Christ. He says this because he who has peace with God does not fear an adverse mind. With God. Or by the angels, who offer them to God. Whence: When you prayed, I offered your prayer to God. Or let them be made known to us before God by endurance, not before men by boasting.
4.7: 4.7 And the peace of God, that is God who is the highest peace, which cannot even be thought, and therefore outside him there is need of none. Which surpasses all understanding. Ours, not theirs who always see the face of the Father. Or the peace by which God himself is at peace surpasses all understanding: except his own, because neither can we know it so, nor any angels.
4.8: 4.8 For the rest, brethren, etc. Hitherto he has admonished against persecutors and against false preachers. For the rest, in conclusion, he sets forth the things that pertain to perfection. Whatsoever things are just. This toward the neighbor. Holy, in one's own life; and to say less, whatsoever things are lovely, that is, worthy to be loved, such as modest bearing, humble speech and the like. Of good fame. AUGUSTINE. For us our life is necessary, for others a good fame. Therefore whoever guards his life from the crimes of wickedness does good to himself; but whoever guards his fame is merciful also to others.
4.10: 4.10 I rejoiced, etc. Here he recalls that they had often sent him what was necessary, whence he shows that their alacrity has been made the more ready, because where they had been negligent, they repeated it with diligence, that, mindful of their apostle, they might send forth fruits to be stored in the heavenly granary. At length, etc. At some time, because they could not at every time. You have flourished again. By ministering to me what was necessary. Which ministry is called a flower, because from it comes the fruit of eternal life. For me. Because your compassion profits me. And lest they seem to have intermitted for some evil cause he adds: now you have flourished again, but before you were occupied and hindered by some adversities.
4.11: 4.11 Not as. Not for himself, but he rejoices at their progress.
4.12: 4.12 I know both how to be abased. He who is not broken by want is not held back from thanksgiving. He who is not kindled by desire of temporal things knows how to be abased, that is to suffer poverty. To abound. He who is not exalted by the things received, who does not twist them to the use of vainglory, who does not possess alone what he has received, but mercifully shares it with the needy, knows how to abound. He who, receiving food, gives not to gorging the belly, nor allots more to the flesh than need demands, knows how to be filled. He who bears the want of food without murmuring, and does nothing out of the necessity of living by which the soul would incur the snare of sin, knows how to be hungry.
4.17: 4.17 Not that I seek. The gift is the thing itself that is given, as a present, food, drink and the like. But the fruit is good works, and the right will of the giver. Whence the Lord in the Gospel does not simply say: He who receives a just man or a prophet, but added: in the name of a just man or a prophet. For to receive a prophet or a just man is a gift. To do this in the name of a just man or a prophet is fruit. Elijah is read to have been fed by a raven and a widow. But through the raven, who fed him not in the name of a just man, it was a gift; through the widow, fruit, because she knew she was feeding a man of God. But fruit. That is, a good and right will joined to good action. For he does not so much rejoice that his need has been relieved as he congratulates their fruitfulness.
4.18: 4.18 For an odor. What was sent by you pleases God as a most sweet odor. They are also compared to prayer, which is the incense of God. Whence it is said: Give alms, and behold all things are clean to you, Luke 11.
4.19: 4.19 May fulfill all your desire. Not in earthly things, but in glory. Or the desires of the saints are filled by the glory of Christ, that Christ himself may thereby be glorious.
